*   ### Beijing First-Time Visitor’s Ultimate Guide to Attractions
Beijing, a city that blends millennia-old charm with modern vitality!
Here, the red walls and yellow tiles of the Forbidden City tell tales of history, the winding Great Wall showcases national spirit, and the trendy buzz of Sanlitun and the CBD pulses with energy.
This guide is specially crafted for first-time visitors, covering must-visit popular attractions and thoughtful tips to help you explore the capital effortlessly and leave no regrets～ 🚩 1.
Popular Attractions in Beijing 🗺️ - 🌟 Tiananmen Square: The symbol and heart of Beijing!
The daily flag-raising ceremony at dawn is solemn and sacred, a must-experience for countless visitors.

On either side of the square stand the Monument to the People’s Heroes and the Chairman Mao Memorial Hall (advance reservation and etiquette compliance required). - 🎭 National Museum of China: The “Cultural Palace” carrying 5,000 years of Chinese civilization!

The museum houses over 1.4 million artifacts, from bronze treasures like the Simuwu Ding and Four-Goat Square Zun to masterpieces such as the “A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains” and “Along the River During the Qingming Festival.” Be sure to book tickets on the official website at least 3 days in advance and allocate 3-4 hours to fully immerse yourself in history. - 🏯 The Forbidden City: The largest and best-preserved wooden ancient architectural complex in the world!

When touring, follow the central axis (Meridian Gate - Hall of Supreme Harmony - Hall of Central Harmony - Hall of Preserving Harmony - Palace of Heavenly Purity - Hall of Union - Imperial Garden) to experience the grandeur of royal architecture.
The Treasure Gallery and Clock and Watch Gallery require separate tickets.
Note that the Forbidden City is closed on Mondays; tickets go on sale at midnight 7 days in advance via the “Palace Museum” mini-program.
It’s recommended to enter from the south gate and exit from the north gate, then visit Jingshan Park for a panoramic view. - 📸 Jingshan Park: The best spot to overlook the entire Forbidden City!
Located opposite the north gate of the Forbidden City, its main peak, Wanchun Pavilion, stands at 47.9 meters.

From the top, enjoy a 360-degree view of Beijing’s urban area, with the red walls and yellow tiles of the Forbidden City to the south, the Bell and Drum Towers to the north, and Beihai Park’s White Pagoda to the west—an excellent vantage point. - 🌉 Shichahai: The most lively historic district in Beijing!
Composed of Qianhai, Houhai, and Xihai lakes, surrounded by attractions like Prince Gong’s Mansion, Yandai Xiejie, and Nanluoguxiang.
In winter, when Shichahai freezes over, you can enjoy ice skating. - 🛍️ Qianmen Street: A commercial street gathering Beijing’s time-honored brands!
The street is lined with quaint traditional buildings and hosts many famous old shops like Quanjude, Tongrentang, and Neiliansheng.
Here you can buy Beijing specialties (such as Peking duck, donkey roll, and pea jelly) and taste various local snacks.

When lanterns light up at night, the atmosphere is perfect for shopping and experiencing old Beijing’s commercial culture. - 🔔 Temple of Heaven Park: The sacred site where emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties worshipped heaven and prayed for good harvests!
Known for its meticulous architectural layout, unique structures, and splendid decorations.

The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, Imperial Vault of Heaven, and Circular Mound Altar are core attractions, especially the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, whose blue glazed tile roof shines brilliantly in the sunlight and is the iconic building of the Temple of Heaven. - 🌿 Summer Palace: The pinnacle of Chinese classical gardens!

Once an imperial garden, based on Kunming Lake and Longevity Hill, it incorporates Jiangnan garden design techniques and is known as the “Royal Garden Museum.” The Long Corridor features over 14,000 paintings.
You can take a boat ride on Kunming Lake to admire the beauty of Longevity Hill and the Seventeen-Arch Bridge from the water.
At sunset, the lake’s scenery is especially enchanting. - 🌧️ Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan): The ruins of the “Garden of Gardens,” bearing witness to history’s weight and vicissitudes!
Although only ruins remain today, the stone pillars of the Western Mansions (Grand Waterworks, Water Viewing Pavilion, and Far-Reaching View Pavilion) still evoke the former glory.
The Yuanmingyuan Exhibition Hall displays the rise and fall of the park through images and artifacts.

It’s recommended to visit with an understanding of the historical context and a respectful heart to appreciate this unique historical imprint. - 🧗 Badaling Great Wall: The classic check-in spot for “He who has never been to the Great Wall is not a true man!” Located in Beijing’s Yanqing District, it is the best-preserved section of the Ming Great Wall.
The wall here is 7.8 meters high and 5.8 meters wide at the top, wide enough for five horses to ride side by side. - 🏅 Bird’s Nest and Water Cube: Iconic venues of the 2008 Beijing Olympics!
The Bird’s Nest (National Stadium) is famous for its unique steel structure design, while the Water Cube (National Aquatics Center) resembles a blue bubble.
Today, these sites host sports events and performances and are popular tourist spots.
You can take photos outside to capture the Olympic spirit.
At night, the Water Cube lights up in a dreamy blue, very beautiful. - 🎢 Universal Studios Beijing: An immersive movie-themed park!
Featuring seven themed areas including the Wizarding World of Harry Potter, Transformers Base, and Minion Land.
It’s recommended to avoid weekends and holidays, enter early in the morning, and follow the guide to hit popular attractions in order.
The evening parade and light show are spectacular, instantly transporting you into a magical movie world. 2.
Important Tips ⚠️ - Museums: Almost all museums (such as the National Museum, Forbidden City, Capital Museum, etc.) require advance reservations, usually through official mini-programs or websites.
Tickets for popular museums are limited, so set alarms to book on time.

Bring your original ID card when entering, follow venue rules, avoid loud noises, and do not touch exhibits. - Hotels must be booked in advance, especially during holidays: As a popular tourist city, hotel prices in Beijing rise sharply during holidays (such as Spring Festival, National Day, and May Day), and availability is tight.
Prioritize hotels near subway stations for convenience.

If on a budget, consider chain hotels or homestays in the city, but check reviews and location carefully. - Watching the flag-raising ceremony: The time adjusts according to Beijing’s sunrise and can be checked on platforms like “Beijing Bendi Bao.” It’s recommended to arrive at Tiananmen Square 1.5-2 hours early, bring your ID, and follow on-site order.

*   ### Exclusive Guide to Winter Family Trips in Beijing

Bringing Kids to Beijing in Winter: Plant a Sprouting Seed of Curiosity Amidst Ice, Snow, and History Bringing kids to Beijing in winter is actually a "hidden gem" – tourist numbers are halved, and attractions are no longer crowded.

The crisp air holds natural classrooms: the snow in the Forbidden City is a "living history book," the aroma of roasted chestnuts in the hutongs is an "enlightenment lesson for life," and the laughter at the ice rink can be etched into childhood memories.
Crucially, children's energy is like a small flame, and winter's slower, warmer pace is perfect for them to gather energy while exploring.

First Stop: The Forbidden City – Turning History into a "Tangible Game" It's hard for children to focus on "explanations" for long, but the Forbidden City's "grandeur" and "wonders" naturally capture their curiosity.

Activity 1: Be a "Little Emperor" for a Day Beforehand, tell your child a simplified version of "An Emperor's Day": attending court in the Palace of Heavenly Purity in the morning, having imperial meals in the Hall of Mental Cultivation at noon (emperors actually ate home-style dishes too), and playing in the Imperial Garden in the afternoon.

Once there, have them count the steps of the Three Great Halls ("Why does the Hall of Supreme Harmony have so many steps?"), look for the "little monsters" on the eaves (Riding Phoenix Immortal, dragon, phoenix... each has a name and purpose), and touch the copper studs on the palace gates ("The more studs on an ancient gate, the more powerful the family").

We recommend bringing a small prop – for example, buying a set of "Ridge Beast Stickers" from the "Forbidden City Stationery Store," so children can find and stick them, like playing a treasure hunt game.

Activity 2: Post-Snow Exclusive – A Collision of Nature and History If it snows, the Forbidden City instantly transforms into a "fairytale kingdom." Step on snow prints with your child ("Let's see whose footprints are bigger, ours or those of ancient officials?"), build a mini "palace" (using branches as beams and snowballs as the roof), and then share a fun fact about "how emperors kept warm on snowy days" (for example, palaces had 'dilong' or underfloor heating, with fire channels beneath the ground).
No problem.

The red walls under the winter sun are a natural "color palette." Let your child use crayons to color "Forbidden City colors" (brick red, bright yellow, bluish-gray) in a sketchbook, which is more meaningful than just taking photos.

Helpful Tip: Go between 9-11 AM when the sun is warm but not harsh; bring a stroller (the Forbidden City paths are flat), and pack some snacks (but don't eat inside the halls); download the "Palace Museum" APP in advance, it has a "family guide" function with audio explanations that sound like storytelling, which children will enjoy.

Second Stop: Hutongs – Learning "Old Beijing Etiquette" Through Everyday Life Hutongs are not "old house museums"; they are windows for children to observe "real life." Choose a few hutongs with a lively atmosphere (such as around Nanluoguxiang, Yandai Xiejie, Yangmeizhu Xiejie), stroll leisurely, and embed "education" in the details.

Activity 1: Be a "Hutong Observer" Give your child a "mission card": find 3 different old door drums (round, square, carved), count how many "Fu" characters are on the doors (some are hidden in brick carvings), and listen for street vendors' calls ("Tanghulu!").
While these are rare now, you might occasionally encounter one.

When you meet a grandpa fixing bicycles or an uncle selling roasted chestnuts, encourage your child to ask a question: "Grandpa, how many years have you been using these tools?" – The kind responses from strangers can teach children "politeness and communication" more effectively than textbooks.

Activity 2: Make "Old Beijing Snacks" Choose a handicraft workshop in a hutong (such as the "Lao She Teahouse" in Qianmen, which offers parent-child experience classes), and take your child to roll tangyuan, make "lǘdagun" (rolling donkey), or learn to make sugar paintings (drawing little rabbits or butterflies on a stone slab with melted sugar syrup).
Eat them on the spot, and your child will proudly say, "Mine tastes better than the store-bought ones!" – The sense of accomplishment from labor lasts longer than any toy.
Avoid This Pitfall: Don't buy overpriced "Old Beijing specialties" (like plastic "Tu'er Ye" figurines) in tourist areas.

Third Stop: Technology and Nature – A "Wonderful Day" at the Ice Rink, Zoo, and Museums Children's energy needs a mix of "activity and quiet," and winter Beijing has so many places to satisfy their natural inclination to "run wild" and be "curious." Fun at the Ice Rink: First Ice Experience The ice rinks at Shichahai or the Summer Palace are children's "happy planets." Choosing an ice sled (a simple sled with a small seat) is safer; parents pull the rope in front, and children shout "Faster!" from behind.
Falling doesn't hurt, and they'll laugh together.
Take the opportunity to share some physics facts: "Why is ice slippery?" "Ice sleds slide because friction is reduced" – learning while playing.

Seeing "Hibernation Reserves" at the Zoo Winter at Beijing Zoo is special: brown bears start accumulating fat (super cute and round), penguins waddle in the greenhouse, and giant pandas munch on bamboo with even more relish (they are less active in winter, making them easier to observe).

Research with your child beforehand: "Which animals hibernate?" "Why aren't penguins afraid of the cold?" Then compare what you learned with what you see on site, which is more vivid than watching documentaries.
Remember to go to the Panda House early in the morning when pandas are more active.

In the National Museum's "Ancient China" exhibition, you can play "artifact puzzles" (like piecing together replicated bronze fragments).

The Science and Technology Museum's "Journey of a Small Ball" allows children to operate mechanical devices firsthand to understand the principles of "gravity" and "gears." If your child is over 5, we recommend booking the "National Museum Parent-Child Tour" (1.5 hours), where guides use a "speaking artifacts" approach to tell history, for example, "This pottery eagle zun was a 'kitchen artifact' from 6,000 years ago." Fourth Stop: Warm Winter Delicacies – Opening Cultural Understanding Through "Eating" Children's stomachs are the most honest "cultural detectors." Beijing's winter cuisine not only warms the body but also tells stories.

Copper Pot Hotpot: A "Sharing Lesson" Around the Stove Choose an old-fashioned restaurant (like Jubaoyuan) and let your child participate in the "hotpot ritual": use a small slotted spoon to scoop a slice of lamb, swirl it in the pot for 10 seconds ("Why shouldn't it cook too long?

Tell your child: "In the past, there were no fresh vegetables in northern winters, so people relied on copper pot hotpot to replenish calories.

Roasted Chestnuts & Sweet Potatoes: Winter's "Olfactory Memory" When passing a roasted chestnut stall, buy a warm bag ("Why are chestnuts roasted?
Because their shells are hard, and roasting makes them easier to peel").
Compete with your child to peel chestnuts, seeing who can peel them whole.

When the aroma of roasted sweet potatoes drifts by, buy one, break it open, and as the golden flesh steams, tell your child: "In the past, there was no heating in winter, and roasted sweet potatoes were the 'hand warmers' of the poor.

"Survival Guide" for Winter Family Trips - Dressing Rules: Layered "onion" style (quick-dry base layer + fleece mid-layer + windproof down jacket); choose fleece-lined sports pants (avoid jeans, which are cold and stiff); shoes should be non-slip (many icy surfaces); wear a wool hat + scarf (to protect ears and neck). - Pace Control: Plan 1-2 main attractions per day (e.g., Forbidden City in the morning, hutongs in the afternoon), leaving 1 hour for "energy release" in between (ice rink or park); if your child is tired, don't push them.

Find a cafe or teahouse to rest, hot drinks + snacks can quickly recharge them. - Health Protection: Pack fever reducers, band-aids, and lip balm (Beijing winters are dry); the temperature difference between indoors and outdoors is significant, so take off hats before entering malls to avoid catching a cold after sweating.
Winter in Beijing is crisply cold and solidly warm.

When bringing children here, there's no need to "check off all attractions." Instead, step on footprints in the snow of the Forbidden City, listen to a street vendor's call in the hutongs, fall on your bottom once at the ice rink, and grab a piece of lamb by the copper pot – these warm fragments will become the "Beijing" in your child's heart: it's not the "capital" from textbooks, but a "grand playground" that can be touched, played with, eaten, and laughed in.
And all we need to do is hold their little hands and say, "Look, this is our history, our life, our winter."

Book tickets in advance on the Forbidden City's official website.

Here you'll find many specialty snacks, creative shops, and bars.

You can eat and stroll, experiencing the blend of Beijing's traditional culture and modern fashion. ● Shichahai: Includes Qianhai, Houhai, and Xihai, three water bodies and their adjacent areas, echoing the "Former Three Seas" and commonly known as the "Latter Three Seas." You can choose to take a boat tour of Shichahai, admire the ancient buildings and scenery along the banks, or stroll by the lake and enjoy a leisurely time. ● Yandai Xiejie: Located on the northeast bank of Qianhai in Shichahai, it is a commercial street with old Beijing charm.
Here you'll find many traditional handicraft shops, tea houses, and snack stalls, where you can buy souvenirs and taste Beijing's specialty snacks.

It is recommended to plan your itinerary and book early. ● When visiting the Mao Zedong Memorial Hall, you must comply with relevant regulations, such as not carrying backpacks, cameras, or other items. ● The Badaling Great Wall is quite steep, so be careful when climbing and wear comfortable shoes. ● When trying Beijing cuisine, pay attention to food hygiene to avoid food poisoning.

Welcome to Shichahai in Beijing!
It is not only rich in historical and cultural heritage, but also a tranquil oasis in the modern city.

Here is a detailed travel guide to help you fully experience the charm of Shichahai. • Introduction to attractions: • Shichahai Park: Shichahai Park consists of three lakes: Qianhai, Houhai, and Xihai.
It is a well-preserved historical scenic area in Beijing.

It not only has charming lake and mountain scenery, but also many former residences of celebrities and ancient sites such as Prince Gong's Mansion and Prince Chun's Mansion. • Yinding Bridge: Located on the waterway between Qianhai and Houhai, it is named for its shape resembling a silver ingot.
Standing on the bridge, you can see the distant Western Hills, which is one of the scenic spots in Shichahai. • Yandai Xie Street: Adjacent to Shichahai, it is 232m long.

There are many specialty shops and delicacies here, making it a great place for tourists to shop and taste food. • Food recommendations: • Makai Restaurant: Located on Gulou Street, it is a popular restaurant in Beijing, with moderate taste and price.
